rules: The table is deliberately approximate and deliberately fixed. Accuracy is not the goal; *agreement* is. Every renderer that implements this table produces the same geometry.
This is why the font stack is part of the spec rather than a theme setting. Change the stack and the 1.06 margin stops being a margin.
No `textLength`, no `dominant-baseline` tricks, no measuring an off-screen node. The SVG is fully positioned before it reaches a browser.

failureModes.when: A title runs past 70 characters
failureModes.then: It wraps to three or four lines and the whole row grows to match — legal, but the box stops scanning

failureModes.when: A note contains an unbreakable 40-character token
failureModes.then: Hard-broken mid-token rather than overflowing

steps.title: Does the workflow declare phases?
steps.note: Phases add a left rail; nothing else changes

detail.purpose: Decide whether to reserve a left margin for phase labels, which is the only place in the entire pipeline where a document-level option changes a coordinate.
procedure: Look for a non-empty `phases` array on the workflow. Each entry names a label and a `from` and `to` step id.

If present, resolve each `from` and `to` to a lane-0 node and record the row range. A phase that names a step which does not exist is an error, not a warning — a mislabelled band is worse than no band.
Sort the resolved phases by their first row, so the rail reads top to bottom regardless of the order they were written in.
Pass a single boolean into the positioning stage: with phases, every lane's x is offset by the rail width; without, it is not.
rules: Phases add no nodes and no edges. They cannot change rows, cannot change lanes, and cannot change which box sits where relative to any other box.
Ranges should be contiguous and non-overlapping over lane 0. Nothing enforces it, but overlapping bands render as overlapping bands and look exactly as wrong as they are.
Phases are worth declaring on any diagram over about ten rows. Below that the reader can hold the whole thing at once and the rail is noise.

failureModes.when: A phase names a step inside a branch
failureModes.then: It resolves to that node's row, and the band covers rows the author did not intend — keep phase endpoints on lane 0

failureModes.when: A phase names a step id that does not exist
failureModes.then: Refused with the phase label quoted

branches.label: No phases declared
branches.note: Skip the rail; the first lane starts at PAD

steps.title: Start the first lane at the page padding
steps.note: x = PAD, with no rail offset

detail.purpose: Keep undecorated diagrams flush left, so a document that declares no phases pays nothing for the feature it did not use.
procedure: Set the starting x to `PAD` — 28 at comfortable density — rather than `PAD + PHASE_RAIL`.
Skip the band geometry entirely. No rail is drawn, no labels are laid out, and the canvas width shrinks by exactly the rail width.
Everything downstream is unchanged: lane widths, gaps, row heights, merge bands, and routing are all computed identically.
rules: This is the only branch in this diagram that rejoins the spine rather than terminating. It skips exactly one step — the band resolution — and picks the pipeline back up at positioning, which is why its exit is a `join` and not a `continue`.

Two diagrams that differ only in whether they declare phases have identical internal geometry, offset by the rail width. That is a property worth preserving, because it means adding phases to an existing diagram never reshapes it.

failureModes.when: Phases are added later
failureModes.then: Every x shifts right by the rail width and nothing else moves at all

steps.title: Resolve each phase to a row range
steps.note: from/to step ids become first and last rows

detail.purpose: Turn author-written step ids into the row numbers the rail is drawn against, now that rows are final and can no longer move.

inputs.label: phases[]
inputs.value: `{ label, from, to }` with step ids

outputs.label: Resolved bands
outputs.value: `{ label, fromRow, toRow }`, sorted by fromRow

procedure: Look each `from` and `to` id up in the step index built during flattening. A miss is an error naming the phase label.
Take each endpoint's final row. This has to happen after the fan-row reservation pass, because reservation can push rows down and a band resolved earlier would be off by however many rows moved.
Sort the bands by first row, so they render top to bottom regardless of the order in the document.
Reserve the rail width on the left. The band itself is drawn as a subtle background stripe spanning the full canvas width, with the label set vertically in the rail.
rules: Bands span the whole canvas, not just lane 0, so a branch that runs deep into the *Draw* phase is visibly still in the Draw phase.
Row ranges are inclusive at both ends.
A phase whose range is a single row is legal and occasionally right — a long, self-contained approval step is a phase of its own.

failureModes.when: Two phases overlap
failureModes.then: Both bands draw and the overlap is visible; nothing refuses, because the intent is occasionally deliberate

failureModes.when: A phase's `to` is above its `from`
failureModes.then: The band inverts and renders as a zero-height stripe

steps.title: Position columns and rows
steps.note: Two independent computations; neither can affect the other
tracks: Columns: x = PAD (+ rail) + Σ lane widths and LANE_GAPs, left to right
Rows: y accumulates row heights plus gutters, top to bottom

detail.purpose: Convert lane indices and row indices into pixels. The two calculations are genuinely independent — nothing about a box's width can affect its row, and nothing about a row's height can affect its column — which is why they are drawn as concurrent tracks.

outputs.label: lane.x, lane.cx, lane.w
outputs.value: Per lane; every node in the lane is centred on `cx`

outputs.label: rowTop[], rowH[]
outputs.value: Per row; every node in the row shares a top edge

outputs.label: width, height
outputs.value: The canvas, sized to fit exactly

procedure: **Columns.** Walk lanes in index order accumulating x. A lane holding at least one node is `NODE_W` wide — 236 at comfortable density; a lane holding only a bypass line gets the narrow `EMPTY_LANE_W` instead, and its centre is offset so the line still lands where a box would have been. Add `LANE_GAP 44` between lanes.
**Rows.** Each row's height is the tallest box in it, computed in the measuring stage. Accumulate downward, adding a gutter between consecutive rows.
Widen any gutter that has to carry more than one merge band: `STUB + (bands − 1) × BAND_GAP + 16`, so stacked bands never overlap each other or the boxes above and below them.
Centre every node horizontally on its lane's centreline and top-align it to its row, then compute the canvas extents from the final lane and the final row.
rules: Every node in a lane shares one x. That is the skewer: a maximal vertical run of boxes threaded on one line, with no box off-axis from the line entering or leaving it.

Lanes are never packed or reused, even when a lane is only occupied for two rows out of forty. Packing would make horizontal position depend on vertical position, and severity would stop being readable off the x-axis.
Vertical growth is free and horizontal growth is expensive — the reason for that asymmetry is that the reader can scroll down without losing the spine, and cannot scroll right without losing it.

failureModes.when: A workflow has more than about twelve lanes
failureModes.then: The canvas exceeds a comfortable screen width; the diagram is not wrong, but it wants splitting

failureModes.when: One box wraps to five lines
failureModes.then: Its whole row grows to match, including every other box in that row

steps.title: Allocate a band in the gutter above each merge target
steps.note: One band per target; stacked by target lane, leftmost on top

detail.purpose: Give every set of merges into the same box one shared horizontal line to travel along, so that three branches rejoining the spine produce one clean band rather than three overlapping horizontals.
procedure: Group every `merge` and `bypass` edge by its target node. Each group gets exactly one band, placed in the gutter immediately above the target's row.
Within one gutter, order the bands by target lane ascending — the leftmost target's band sits topmost — and then by node index to break ties deterministically.
Record each band's horizontal extent from the leftmost source to the target's centreline, so the drawn segment is exactly as long as it needs to be and no longer.
Widen the gutter to fit: a gutter with `n` bands is at least `STUB + (n − 1) × BAND_GAP + 16` tall, where `BAND_GAP` is 14 at comfortable density.
rules: Bands live above their target, never below. That follows directly from the direction check: every merge points downward, so its target is always below every source, and the gutter above the target is always free of the sources' boxes.
Ordering by target lane is what keeps stacked bands from crossing each other. Two bands in one gutter with targets in different lanes are nested, not interleaved.
A band with one source is still a band. Uniform treatment costs a few pixels and removes an entire class of special case from the router.

failureModes.when: Four branches merge into one step
failureModes.then: One band with four drops into it, and a gutter roughly 40px taller than the default

failureModes.when: Two bands in a gutter have targets in the same lane
failureModes.then: Ordered by node index; deterministic, and geometrically identical either way

steps.title: Route every edge as right angles
steps.note: Down, right, or left to merge — nothing else

detail.purpose: Convert the node positions and band allocations into actual path geometry: straight segments and right angles, nothing diagonal and nothing curved except the rounded corner where a line turns.
procedure: A sequential edge is one vertical line down the lane.
A fan edge leaves the question's right vertex, runs right along that row, and drops into the branch's column.
A merge edge drops down its own lane to the band above its target, runs left, and enters the target's top edge.
Corners are rounded by a fixed radius so a turn reads as one line rather than two.
rules: Every segment is horizontal or vertical. There are no diagonals.
Crossings are not routed around at this stage — they are prevented earlier, by the column ordering and the row reservation, and anything left over is caught by the check that follows.

failureModes.when: A band crosses several drops
failureModes.then: One hop per crossing, all on the band rather than on the drops, so the vertical lines stay unbroken

failureModes.when: A fan spans eight lanes
failureModes.then: One long horizontal with eight drops — legal and readable, but a sign the question is really a choice with a table behind it

steps.title: Emit the SVG into a self-contained page
steps.note: Same document in, same bytes out
steps.destination: One HTML file: diagrams, modals, source, renderer, prompt

detail.purpose: Serialise the finished geometry and assemble the page — every diagram, every modal, the document that produced them, the renderer, and the prompt — into one file with no external dependencies.

outputs.label: SVG
outputs.value: One per workflow, fully positioned, with explicit tspans

outputs.label: HTML
outputs.value: Self-contained page: CSS, JS, modal payloads, embedded source, embedded prompt

procedure: Emit each node as its shape — rectangle, hexagon, trapezoid, right- and left-slanted parallelograms, split rectangle, double-side-barred rectangle, clipped-corner rectangle, double-top-and-bottom-barred rectangle, stadium — with the wrapped tspans already positioned.
Emit the paths, the fan labels, the phase rail, the display numbers, and the chips. Chips carry the resolved target so they can scroll and flash it on click.
Serialise each step's `detail` into the page as the modal payload, rendered according to the workflow's lens.
Inline everything: stylesheet, script, the complete WFD source, and the master prompt. No CDN, no fetch, no font download. The finished page opens from `file://` on a machine with no network.
Print a one-line summary — diagram count, step count, and how many steps rendered with no detail. That last number is the only quality metric the renderer can compute, and it should be zero.
rules: Determinism is the deliverable. The same document produces the same bytes on any machine, which is what lets a diagram live in version control and be reviewed in a pull request like code.
Nothing in the pipeline consults the clock, the locale, a random source, or the DOM. If two renders of one document differ, that is a bug in the renderer, not a variation.

The page carries its own source and its own prompt on purpose. An artefact that can regenerate itself, and can teach a reader to make the next one, does not need the site it came from to keep existing.

failureModes.when: A step has no `detail`
failureModes.then: It renders, the modal opens empty, and the summary line counts it — which is the number to drive to zero

failureModes.when: The page is several hundred KB
failureModes.then: Normal; that weight is modal prose, and it is the part worth carrying

end.label: One self-contained page · byte-identical every time
end.note: No network, no build step, no server at the reading end

workflows.title: Choose how a branch ends
workflows.description: Every branch has to terminate, and there are exactly five ways to do it. Choosing wrongly is the one authoring mistake that produces a document which validates and is still wrong. This is that decision as a diagram: eight questions, asked in order of how much the answer costs, with the trap that catches most people sitting near the top.

summary.trigger: You have written a branch — the steps someone takes when a question does not go the good way — and now it has to end somewhere
summary.outcome: One of `continue`, `join`, `goback`, `goto`, or `end`, chosen for a reason you could defend to someone reading the diagram in a year
summary.owner: Whoever is authoring the document, model or human
summary.duration: under a minute per branch, once you have walked it twice
summary.frequency: Once per branch — the most-repeated decision in the format

start.label: A branch exists and has to end somewhere
start.note: A dangling branch is not legal; there are exactly five endings

steps.title: Say out loud what happens and what happens next
steps.note: Two clauses; if you need three, it is two branches

detail.purpose: Force the branch into a single sentence before choosing an ending, because the ending is almost always obvious from the sentence and almost never obvious from the JSON.
procedure: Write one sentence in exactly this shape: *when X happens, we do Y, and then Z.* For example, *when the card is declined, we ask for another card, and then we try the payment again.*

Look at the *and then* clause. It is the exit. "...and then we try the payment again" points back up the diagram; "...and then we carry on" points at the next step; "...and then we're done, the order is cancelled" points at nothing.
If your sentence needs three clauses, or contains the word *unless*, you have two branches tangled together and the ending you pick will be wrong for one of them.
Write the sentence down somewhere. It is the first line of the branch's `detail.purpose`, and you have just written it.
rules: The exit is a property of the process, not a stylistic choice. There is a correct answer, and the sentence contains it.
Branch labels name the **answer**, not the consequence. `"Declined"`, `"Timeout"`, `"No"` — never `"Go to error handling"`. The label says what happened; the exit says where it goes.
If you cannot say what happens next, you have found something real: nobody knows. Say that in `detail.rules` and route it to a human. An honest unknown is worth more than a confident guess.

failureModes.when: The sentence has two *and then* clauses
failureModes.then: Two branches; split the question

failureModes.when: The *and then* clause is a paragraph
failureModes.then: The branch is a process, not a detour

steps.title: Is this one deviation rather than two?
steps.note: If the label needs "and" or "or", it is two

detail.purpose: Catch tangled branches before choosing an exit, because a branch that covers two situations will need two different endings and you will pick the one that suits the situation you thought of first.
procedure: Read the branch label. If it contains *and*, *or*, or a slash, it is covering more than one answer.
Read the branch's steps. If the first two steps only make sense in one situation and the last two only make sense in another, the branch is two branches sharing a lane.
Read the question that owns it. A question whose title contains *and* is two questions, and its branches will inherit the tangle no matter how carefully you label them.
Ask whether both situations end the same way. Two situations that share every step *and* the same ending are genuinely one branch with a two-word label — that case is fine.
rules: One question, one decision. This is the rule that prevents most of the others from being needed.
Two questions in a row on the spine cost one row each and read cleanly. One question with a compound label costs nothing and reads wrong forever.
A `choice` with named answers is the right shape when several situations are genuinely alternatives at the same moment; two stacked questions are right when they happen at different moments.

failureModes.when: The two situations need different endings
failureModes.then: Definitive — split them

failureModes.when: There are five or more situations
failureModes.then: It is a `choice`, not a stack of questions

branches.label: Two tangled together
branches.note: Different situations, different endings, one lane

steps.title: Split it into two questions on the spine
steps.note: Stacked, not nested — depth is more expensive than height

detail.purpose: Turn one compound gate into two simple ones so that each branch has exactly one situation and therefore exactly one correct ending.
procedure: Write both questions out separately, each with a yes/no answer where the good answer is the primary one and continues down the spine.
Put them **in sequence on lane 0**, not nested. Stacking costs one extra row; nesting costs a whole lane and pushes every later branch further right.
Order them by which is asked first in real life. If both are checked at the same moment against the same data, they are probably one `choice` with named answers rather than two questions.
Now re-run this decision separately for each branch. That is the point of the split: two questions, two branches, two endings, each obviously right.
rules: Prefer height to depth, always. A diagram twice as tall is legible; a diagram one lane wider costs 280 pixels and pushes everything to its right.
After splitting, check the polarity of both questions. A compound question often hid an inverted one, and an inverted question puts the happy path on the wrong side.
Two questions with the same branch steps are a sign you split on the wrong axis. Re-read the sentence from the first step.

failureModes.when: The split produces two identical branches
failureModes.then: It was one question after all; merge them and give the branch a two-word label

failureModes.when: The second question only applies inside the first branch
failureModes.then: That one is genuinely nested — accept one lane of depth

steps.title: Will the branch fit in five steps or fewer?
steps.note: A branch longer than five steps is a diagram, not a detour

detail.purpose: Ask the length question before the ending question, because a branch that is too long has already answered the ending question — it is going to be a `goto`, and everything you decide about `continue` versus `join` first will be wasted.
procedure: Count the steps you would need to write. Not the steps you have written — the steps the situation actually requires, including the ones you were about to summarise into one box.

Five is the ceiling and it is not arbitrary: a six-step branch is taller than most spines, it drags its lane down past everything it is supposed to be an exception to, and the renderer warns about it by name.

Check the other two promotion signals while you are here. Does it have its own trigger — something that starts it from outside, rather than something that happened on this spine? Does it have a different owner *and* a different success condition? Either is enough on its own.
If it is long, stop working the exit decision. The branch is a workflow, and its ending is decided by whether control comes back.
rules: This is the trap the whole diagram exists to spring. Most badly shaped documents are not documents with wrong exits; they are documents with one branch that should have been a diagram, and every wrong exit downstream is a consequence of that.
The preference order is: `continue` over `join`, `join` over `goback`, `goback` over a new diagram, and a new diagram over a twelve-step branch. The last of those is the only one that is absolute.
Length is a proxy for independence. A branch that needs six steps is doing work that has its own beginning and its own end, whatever you call it.

failureModes.when: You compress six steps into three boxes to stay under the ceiling
failureModes.then: You have hidden the process rather than shortened it — the boxes will not survive the modal review

failureModes.when: The branch is exactly five steps and growing
failureModes.then: Promote it now; branches only ever grow

branches.label: Six or more
branches.note: It has its own beginning and its own end — it is a diagram

steps.title: Promote it to a workflow of its own
steps.note: Then decide: does control come back?

detail.purpose: Move the branch out into a diagram with its own trigger, outcome, and summary, and leave behind a single reference in the place it used to sprawl.
detail.duration: one more pass over the document
procedure: Give the new workflow a trigger and an outcome, both stated as things that happen in the world. If you cannot state a trigger different from the caller's, the branch is not independent and should be collapsed instead of promoted.

Decide whether control returns. **If it does**, the branch becomes an `insert` step on the spine and the box itself is the link — nothing terminates, and the reader knows the spine continues after it. **If it does not**, the branch keeps whatever steps run before the handoff and terminates in a `goto` chip.
Give the promoted workflow its own `summary` and, if it is long, its own phases. It is a diagram now, not a fragment.
Place it in the document after the workflow that references it. Document order is reading order and it sets the diagram numbers that every chip is labelled with.
rules: `insert` when control returns; `goto` when it does not. Getting this backwards makes the diagram lie about whether anything happens afterwards, and it is the one lie readers do not catch.
Two to six workflows is comfortable. More than eight usually means you split on data variation — enterprise versus self-serve — rather than on process variation.

The promoted diagram needs its own exit decisions for its own branches. That is why this branch leaves for diagram 1 rather than looping back here: you are starting a document, not finishing a branch.

failureModes.when: The promoted workflow has three steps
failureModes.then: It was not independent; inline it and collapse the nesting instead

failureModes.when: Two workflows now goto each other
failureModes.then: One of them is really an `insert` — find the one where control comes back

links.label: The authoring loop, from the top

steps.title: Does the branch do any work of its own?
steps.note: Some answers only mean "skip the next bit"

detail.purpose: Recognise the branch that has no steps at all — the pure bypass — because it is legal, cheap, and consistently written as a one-step branch containing a box that says nothing.
procedure: Ask what someone actually *does* on this branch. If the honest answer is "nothing — we just skip the verification and carry on", the branch has no steps.

Watch for the placeholder box. `"Skip verification"`, `"Do nothing"`, `"Proceed"` and `"No action required"` are all the same non-step, and each of them will fail the modal review because there is nothing to write in it.
Leave `steps` as an empty array and give the branch a real `exit` and a real `note`. The note is where the explanation goes — it renders on the canvas next to the answer label.
Check the exit carefully, because a bypass is exactly the case where `continue` and `join` differ. Skipping *the next step* is a `join` further down; carrying straight on is a `continue`.
rules: An empty branch renders as a single line leaving the question and merging into its target, drawn in a narrow column rather than a full-width one. It is the cheapest thing in the notation.
A branch whose only step would restate the branch label is a bypass. Delete the box.
Bypasses still need a `note` if the reason is not obvious from the label. The note is one muted line on the canvas and it is often the most-read text in the diagram.

failureModes.when: The 'nothing' turns out to be a state change
failureModes.then: It is a `shelf` step and it belongs on the branch after all

failureModes.when: The bypass skips three steps
failureModes.then: That is a `join`, and the note should say what is being skipped and why

branches.label: Nothing happens
branches.note: A pure bypass — this branch of this question is one

steps.title: Leave the steps array empty and write the note
steps.note: The note carries what the missing box would have said

detail.purpose: Express "skip this part" as an empty branch with a good note, rather than as a box containing a restatement of its own label.
procedure: Set `"steps": []`. This is legal and expected; the renderer emits a single bypass edge from the question straight to the merge target.

Write a `note` on the branch of at most about 80 characters, saying what is being skipped and why. It renders under the answer label, on the line, where a reader scanning the right margin will see it.

Choose the exit deliberately. `continue` means *carry on from the next step*; `join` means *skip ahead to this named step*. For a bypass those are usually different things and it is easy to write the first while meaning the second.
Do not add a `detail` — there is no box to open. Everything the reader needs is in the label and the note.
rules: The empty lane still consumes a lane index, but renders narrow. Bypasses are cheap in width; steps are not.
If you find yourself wanting a modal on a bypass, the branch does do something and you should give it a step.
This branch is itself an example: there is nothing to do about a bypass except recognise it, so the decision continues at the next question.

failureModes.when: The note has to explain three things
failureModes.then: The bypass is hiding a step; write the step

steps.title: Does it pick the spine back up at the very next step?
steps.note: The default answer, and the one to reach for first

detail.purpose: Test for the commonest ending first, because it is the cheapest to write, the cheapest to read, and the only one that never needs maintaining when a step id changes.
procedure: Read the *and then* clause of your sentence. If it is "...and then we carry on as normal", this is a `continue`.

Check what "the next step" actually means here: the step immediately after the question that owns this branch, in the owning lane. If the question is the last step of its lane, it means that lane's own ending — which chains, and is usually what you want.
Prefer `continue` to `join` whenever both would work. `continue` names no target, so it cannot rot when a step id changes, and it survives someone inserting a step above it.
If a `join` you wrote points at exactly the step after the question, rewrite it as a `continue`. Same geometry, one fewer name to keep in sync.
rules: `continue` is the default. The order of preference is `continue`, then `join`, then `goback`, then a new diagram — and every step down that list costs the reader something.
`continue` produces a merge line and no extra box, exactly like `join`. The difference is entirely in what has to stay true for the document to keep validating.

A recovery branch that fixes the problem and carries on is nearly always a `continue`. A recovery branch that has to re-run the failed step is a `goback` — the distinction is whether the failed step needs doing again.

failureModes.when: It rejoins two steps further down
failureModes.then: That is a `join`, and it should skip visibly

failureModes.when: It re-runs the step that failed
failureModes.then: That is a `goback`, not a rejoin

branches.label: Yes, immediately after
branches.note: No target to name and nothing to keep in sync

exit.label: Use continue
exit.note: { "type": "continue" } — merges into the step after the question

steps.title: Does it pick the spine back up further down?
steps.note: Skipping over steps that no longer apply

detail.purpose: Handle the branch that rejoins the main route but skips part of it — the customer who paid by invoice and therefore misses three payment steps — which is a `join` and needs a named target.
procedure: Identify the step where this branch's work stops mattering and the shared route resumes. That is the join target.

Verify the target is in an **ancestor lane**: the branch's own lane, or its parent's, up to lane 0. A target inside a sibling branch is never legal, because the two lanes are only related through their shared question.
Verify the target is **below** the branch's last step once rows are assigned. If it is not, this is a back-reference and belongs to the next question, not this one.
Name the skipped steps in the branch's `note`. A join is a visible skip on the canvas, and the reader will want to know what was skipped without opening anything.
rules: `join` names a target, so it is the first exit type that can rot. If someone renames the target step, the document stops validating — which is the good outcome, but it is still maintenance.
A join into a sibling branch is the most common illegal exit people write. The fix is nearly always that both branches should merge into a shared step on the spine instead.
If the skip covers more than about three steps, check whether those steps should be a sub-workflow reached by `insert` on the main route, with this branch simply continuing past it.

failureModes.when: The target is above the branch
failureModes.then: Refused by the direction check with a goback replacement quoted

failureModes.when: The target is in a sibling branch
failureModes.then: Refused on the lane rule; merge both into a shared spine step instead

branches.label: Yes, further down
branches.note: Ancestor lane, strictly below — check both

steps.title: Check the target is an ancestor and below
steps.note: Both conditions, or it is not a join

detail.purpose: Verify the two conditions that make a `join` legal, before the renderer does it for you, because the failure mode reads like a layout complaint and is actually a modelling error.
procedure: **Ancestor.** Walk up from your branch: your lane, the lane of the question that owns it, that lane's owner, up to lane 0. The target must be in one of those. Anything else — a sibling branch, a cousin, a branch of a different question — is refused.

**Below.** The target must lay out strictly below the branch's last step. Rows come from longest-path layering, so "below" usually matches "later in the document", but a branch with several steps can reach further down than you expect.
Write the note. "Invoice customers skip card capture, authorisation, and settlement" is worth more to a reader than the geometry ever will be.
Sanity-check by reading the diagram out loud: *when the customer is on invoice terms, we tag the account, and then we carry on from fulfilment.* If that sentence is true, the join is right.
rules: Ancestor **and** below. Both, every time. One without the other is a different exit type.
If the target is the immediate next step, use `continue` instead — same result, no name to maintain.
If you want to join into a sibling branch, what you actually want is for both branches to merge into a shared step on their common ancestor lane. Add that step.

failureModes.when: Both conditions hold but the diagram looks wrong
failureModes.then: The skip is real but too large; the skipped run probably wants to be an insert on the spine

steps.title: Does it send the reader back up the diagram?
steps.note: Every retry, resubmit, and poll lives here

detail.purpose: Catch every loop in the process, because loops cannot be drawn — there are no upward lines — and must be converted into a terminal chip before the document is written.
procedure: Ask whether anything gets *done again*. Retry the payment, ask for the address again, poll the vendor once more, resubmit after correcting the form: all of these return to a step that already ran.
Identify the exact step you go back to. It is nearly always the step that failed, or the input step just before it — rarely anything else.
Verify the target is at or above the branch's last step. If it is below, this is a forward skip and belongs to the previous question, and the renderer will say so with the join replacement quoted.

Write a `label` on the chip if the auto-generated one is not enough. The default renders as `↩ Go back to 3 · Validate the cart`, which is usually right; `Retry with the corrected address` is better when the reason matters more than the destination.
rules: A `goback` chip is a dead end on the canvas. The line stops there and the reader's eye never travels upward — the chip is clickable and scrolls to its target instead.
State the loop bound somewhere. "Three attempts, then hand to a human" belongs in `detail.rules` on the step being retried, because the chip itself cannot express a count.

This is the one place the notation is knowingly worse than DRAKON. DRAKON's loop icons make repetition traceable with a fingertip; a chip makes it a lookup. We took that trade to allow retries to arbitrary earlier points, and it is worth knowing you are paying it.

failureModes.when: The target is below the chip
failureModes.then: Refused as a forward merge, with the join replacement quoted

failureModes.when: The retry has no bound
failureModes.then: Not a validation error, but an unbounded loop in a real process — write the bound and the escape into the rules

branches.label: Yes, back up
branches.note: Retry, resubmit, poll — all the same shape

steps.title: Check the target is at or above, then bound the loop
steps.note: And say what happens on the last attempt

detail.purpose: Make the back-reference legal and make the loop finite, which are two different problems that arrive together and only one of which the validator can see.
procedure: Confirm the target lays out at or above the branch's last step. Anything strictly below is a forward merge and the renderer refuses it, quoting the `join` replacement.

Pick the target precisely. Going back to the *input* step usually means the data was wrong; going back to the *action* step usually means the attempt was wrong. They read very differently to someone following the diagram.
Bound the loop. Write the attempt count and the escape into `detail.rules` on the step you return to: *three attempts at 2s, 8s, 30s; after the third, the case goes to the review queue.*
Then check that the escape exists in the diagram. An unbounded retry with no drawn escape is the most common way a diagram quietly disagrees with reality.
rules: The chip cannot carry a count and it should not try. Loop bounds live in the modal of the step being retried.
If the escape after N attempts is a whole procedure, it is a second branch on the same question — usually the rightmost one, because running out of retries is the worst answer.
Two chips pointing at the same target from different branches are fine and common. They are references, not edges, so they cost nothing structurally.

failureModes.when: There is no escape from the retry
failureModes.then: Add the branch that fires when the attempts run out, at the same question, on the right

failureModes.when: The chip points at a step in another workflow
failureModes.then: That is a `goto`, not a `goback` — gobacks are always within one diagram

exit.label: Use goback
exit.note: { "type": "goback", "to": "..." } — a chip, at or above, clickable

steps.title: Is it really a different process from here on?
steps.note: Its own trigger, its own outcome, its own owner

detail.purpose: Separate a detour from a handoff. A detour comes back and belongs on this diagram; a handoff does not, and drawing it here is what turns a readable spine into a general graph.
procedure: Apply three tests. **Trigger:** does something start it from outside this spine? **Outcome:** does "done and good" mean something different from this workflow's outcome? **Owner:** is a different team or role responsible from here on? Two of three is enough.

Then ask the question that decides which reference to use: does control come back? A fraud review that returns a verdict and lets the order continue is an `insert`. An order that is cancelled and becomes a refund case is a `goto`.

For a `goto`, keep any steps that run *before* the handoff on this branch, then terminate in the chip. "Notify the customer, close the case, then go to diagram 4" is three boxes and a chip, not just a chip.
Name the target workflow, and the target step if there is a specific entry point. The chip renders as `↗ Go to diagram 2 · Refund flow` and is clickable.
rules: `insert` is a call: control returns and the spine continues below it. `goto` is a handoff: control does not return and the branch is over. The reader relies on this distinction absolutely.

This is where the notation diverges from DRAKON, which only has the call. A one-way jump makes the multi-diagram document a general graph rather than a call tree, so "does this ever come back?" stops being answerable from the shape — which is exactly why the two references look different.
If you find yourself wanting a `goto` back to a diagram that gotos you, one of the two is an `insert`. Find the one where control returns.

failureModes.when: Only one of the three tests passes
failureModes.then: It is a detour; keep it here and pick a merge exit

failureModes.when: Control does come back
failureModes.then: It is an `insert` step on the spine, not a branch exit at all

branches.label: Yes, and it does not return
branches.note: Different trigger, different outcome, different owner

steps.title: Decide once whether control comes back
steps.note: Comes back: insert on the spine. Does not: goto chip

detail.purpose: Make the call-versus-handoff decision explicitly and once, because it is the only structural fact about a cross-diagram link and readers will believe whatever the diagram says.
procedure: Ask the plain question: after the other process finishes, does anything happen on *this* spine? If yes, it is a call. If the case is over as far as this workflow is concerned, it is a handoff.

**Call.** Put an `insert` step on the spine — usually on lane 0, not on a branch — naming the workflow, and optionally the entry step. The box is a link and the spine continues below it. This is the shape used for sub-processes that return a verdict.
**Handoff.** Keep the steps that run before the departure on the branch, then end it with a `goto` chip naming the workflow and, if useful, the step.
Then check the other diagram exists in the same document. Both references resolve at validation time, and a chip pointing at a workflow that is not in the document is refused.
rules: Both references live in one document. There is no cross-file linking; if two workflows reference each other they ship together, which is deliberate.
A `goto` may name a specific entry step, but the target workflow still has exactly one `start`. The chip scrolls the reader to the step; it does not create a second entry point.

Diagram numbers in chip labels are positional, taken from document order. Reordering workflows renumbers the chips — which is fine, because the renderer regenerates the labels, and is a good reason never to hand-write a diagram number into a title.

failureModes.when: You want both — it returns sometimes
failureModes.then: Two different situations; split the question and give each its own reference

failureModes.when: The target workflow does not exist yet
failureModes.then: Write it. Both reference types are refused at validation if the target is missing

exit.label: Use goto — or insert, if it returns
exit.note: { "type": "goto", "workflow": "..." } — a chip; an insert is a step, not an exit

steps.title: Does the path genuinely finish here?
steps.note: Including "a human owns it now and we are done"

detail.purpose: Confirm the last remaining answer rather than defaulting to it, because `end` is what people reach for when they have stopped thinking, and a wrongly terminated branch silently claims a process is over when it is not.
procedure: Ask whether anything at all happens afterwards *within this workflow's responsibility*. If a queue picks it up tomorrow and this workflow's owner never touches it again, it genuinely finishes here.
Write the `label` as an outcome someone could verify from outside: *Refund denied · customer notified*, not *Error* and not *Exit*.

Set the `tone` honestly. `failure` for a genuine bad outcome, `neutral` for a legitimate non-success like a handoff to a person, `success` for an outcome that is fine even though it left the spine early.
Add a `note` saying what the reader should know about the aftermath — who owns it now, what the customer sees, what gets written down.
rules: "Hand it to a human and we are done" is a real ending, with tone `neutral`. It is not a failure and it should not be coloured like one.
An `end` stadium is the only exit with no target, which is why it is the easiest to write and the easiest to write wrongly. If you cannot name the observable outcome, the path does not end here.

The workflow's own `end` — the one at the bottom of lane 0 — is different from a branch `end`. Lane 0's ending is the outcome the whole workflow exists to produce, and it should almost always have tone `success`.

failureModes.when: Something does happen afterwards
failureModes.then: You have not found the exit yet — start again from the sentence

failureModes.when: The label is 'Error' or 'Exit'
failureModes.then: Name the outcome instead; a stadium that says 'Error' teaches the reader nothing

branches.label: No, something follows
branches.note: Then one of the four above is the answer — go again

steps.title: Rewrite the sentence and walk it again
steps.note: The and-then clause was missing or wrong

detail.purpose: Send the author back to the one artefact that determines the answer, rather than letting them pick an ending by elimination when the elimination has failed.
procedure: Reaching this point means all five endings were rejected, which is not possible for a well-described branch. The sentence is wrong, not the decision.

Rewrite it with a real *and then* clause. The commonest defect is a sentence that ends at the deviation — *when the card is declined, we ask for another card* — and never says what happens after that.
If the honest continuation is "and then it depends", you have a second question hiding inside the branch. Add it as a question **inside** the branch, with its own branches and its own endings.
Then walk this diagram again from the top. The second pass takes about thirty seconds and almost always lands.
rules: A branch that cannot be ended is a branch that has not been described. This is a description problem every time.
Do not resolve it by picking `end`. A wrongly terminated branch is the one error that neither the validator nor a reader will catch, because a stadium looks finished.
If two passes both fail, the branch is a process. Promote it and give it its own diagram.

failureModes.when: The second pass also fails
failureModes.then: Promote the branch; it is a workflow

failureModes.when: The continuation depends on something not yet asked
failureModes.then: Add a question inside the branch and end each of its branches separately

exit.label: Rewrite the sentence and go again

end.label: Use end — a terminal stadium with a verifiable outcome
end.note: Name the outcome, set the tone honestly, say who owns it now
